stories.title: Nobody Found The Manhole Cover A Nuke Launched
stories.description: In 1957 a nuclear safety test in Nevada fired a welded steel cap up a borehole at an estimated six times Earth's escape velocity. One camera frame is the only proof it ever moved, and the cap was never recovered. #unsolvedmysteries #bizarrehistory #nuclearhistory

factual_claims.text: No one ever recovered the steel cap launched up the shaft by the Pascal-B test at the Nevada Test Site on 27 August 1957.
Pascal-B yielded roughly 300 tons, far more than intended, and the blast travelled up the borehole.
A high-speed camera running about one frame per millisecond captured the steel cap in only a single frame.
Robert Brownlee of Los Alamos estimated the cap's velocity at about six times Earth's escape velocity, and it was never recovered.
Scientists believe compression heating vaporised the cap during its flight out through the atmosphere.

segments.narration: Nobody ever found the manhole cover a nuclear test launched. Nevada, August 27th, 1957. A two-thousand-pound steel lid, welded over a borehole.
Underneath sat a bomb meant to barely fizzle. It yielded about three hundred tons instead. The shaft became a gun barrel.
A camera shooting a thousand frames a second caught the lid in exactly one frame. One. So how fast was it moving?
Los Alamos physicist Robert Brownlee ran the numbers and got six times Earth's escape velocity. He never recovered the cap.
It almost certainly never reached space. Compression heating would have vaporised the steel on the way up, which means the fastest thing humans had ever made burned itself out of existence.

research.summary: Pascal-B, 27 August 1957, was an underground shaft safety experiment in Operation Plumbbob (28 May - 7 October 1957, Nevada Test Site, 29 detonations). A steel lid of roughly 900 kg was welded over the borehole. The device yielded about 300 tons, far above expectation; the blast drove the lid up the shaft and out. A high-speed camera running one frame per millisecond caught it in a single frame, from which Los Alamos physicist Robert Brownlee estimated about six times Earth's escape velocity (~66-67 km/s). The cap was never found; compression heating is believed to have vaporised it. Popular sources disagree on the exact figure (modern re-estimates near 56 km/s) and some transpose Pascal-A and Pascal-B details, so the script attributes the number to Brownlee rather than stating it as settled.

segments.narration: Four people broke into the Pantheon to repair its clock. Paris, the mid-2000s. Nobody hired them, and nobody asked.
Its clock had sat dead since the 1960s. So they built a workshop up under the dome and worked there for about a year.
One of them, Jean-Baptiste Viot, was a professional clockmaker. He took the mechanism apart piece by piece. Who breaks in to do unpaid maintenance?
They call themselves Untergunther, part of a Paris underground network that quietly restores neglected heritage. When the clock ran again, they went and told the management themselves.
France took them to court for it. The judge ruled in their favour in about twenty minutes, and years later Viot won the official contract to restore the same clock.

segments.narration: Sardinia has seven thousand stone towers and no written explanation. They are called nuraghi. Cones of stacked dark stone, the tallest about twenty metres.
They went up in the Bronze Age, from roughly the eighteenth century BC onward. Individual blocks run to several tons each.
Nothing bonds them. The walls hold on the weight of their own stones, leaning inward until they close into a dome overhead. And nobody knows what they were for.
Fortresses. Chiefs' houses. Temples. Meeting halls. Archaeologists have argued every one of those, and there is still no agreement.
Then a 2002 survey measured the doorways. A great many of them face the winter solstice sunrise, which means whatever else these towers were, somebody was lining them up with the sky.

research.summary: Nuraghi are Bronze Age dry-stone towers unique to Sardinia; more than 7,000 have been found and archaeologists estimate over 10,000 were built, from the middle Bronze Age (18th-15th c. BCE) to the Late Bronze Age, with the nuragic period usually given as 1900-730 BC. The structure holds on the weight of its stones, each up to several tons, with an inward-tilted outer layer and a corbelled tholos dome; some reach about 20 m and Nuraghe Arrubiu 25-30 m. There is no consensus on function - rulers' residences, strongholds, meeting halls, temples, dwellings or a mix - and Su Nuraxi di Barumini, the most complete example, was inscribed by UNESCO in 1997. A 2002 study by Belmonte and Zedda found many entrances align with the winter solstice sunrise and the southernmost moonrise.

factual_claims.text: In April 2019 fishermen near Hammerfest in northern Norway found a beluga whale wearing a tight-fitting harness.
The harness had a mount for a GoPro camera but no camera, and its clasp was marked 'Equipment St Petersburg'.
The whale played fetch, retrieved a kayaker's dropped camera from the harbour floor, and responded to hand gestures.
The name Hvaldimir combines the Norwegian word 'hval' with Vladimir; Russia never confirmed involvement, and a Russian military commentator did not rule out that the whale escaped from the navy.
He was found dead at Risavika near Stavanger on 31 August 2024; the necropsy found no projectiles and pointed to a bacterial infection, probably from a stick lodged in his mouth.

segments.narration: A beluga whale showed up wearing a harness labelled St Petersburg. Off Hammerfest, northern Norway, April 2019. It came straight up to the fishing boats.
The harness was tight-fitting, with a mount for a GoPro and no camera in it. The clasp read Equipment St Petersburg.
He played fetch. He brought a kayaker's dropped camera back up off the harbour floor. He answered hand signals. So who trained him?
Norway named him Hvaldimir, from hval, whale, plus Vladimir. Russia never confirmed a thing, and one Russian military commentator would not rule out a navy escape.
He was found dead near Stavanger in August 2024. No bullets: the post-mortem pointed at infection from a stick lodged in his mouth. Who sent him out is still unanswered.

research.summary: In April 2019 fishermen near Hammerfest, Norway, found a beluga in a tight camera harness whose buckle read 'Equipment St Petersburg' and which carried a GoPro mount but no camera. The whale sought out boats, played fetch, retrieved a kayaker's GoPro from the harbour floor and responded to hand gestures, implying prior training. Verdens Gang coined the name Hvaldimir (Norwegian 'hval' plus Vladimir) and an NRK public vote made it official. Russia never confirmed involvement; military commentator Viktor Baranets questioned the spy theory but did not rule out an escape from the Russian Navy, and a Ukrainian researcher claimed he was captured in 2013 and escaped from Murmansk. He was found dead at Risavika near Stavanger on 31 August 2024. The necropsy found no projectiles; the Veterinary Institute attributed death to bacterial infection, probably from a stick lodged in his mouth, and police opened no criminal case. NOAH and OneWhale dispute that conclusion.

factual_claims.text: The Yonaguni formation lies about 26 metres deep off Yonaguni Island in Japan's Ryukyu Islands and was noticed in 1986.
Kihachiro Aratake, a local tourism association director, spotted the formation while looking for hammerhead sharks.
Masaaki Kimura of the University of the Ryukyus argued the formation is man-made, identifying a pyramid, roads and a stadium.

segments.narration: Twenty-six metres down off Japan sits a stone staircase. Yonaguni, the far western tip of the Ryukyu Islands. A diver found it in 1986.
Flat terraces. Right angles. Walls that look cut. Kihachiro Aratake was out looking for hammerhead sharks when he swam into the thing.
A Ryukyu University geologist, Masaaki Kimura, called it a sunken city. Pyramids, roads, a stadium. Was there a lost civilisation under Japan?
Other geologists dived it and found the answer in the rock itself. Sandstone, about twenty million years old, sliced through by parallel bedding planes and vertical fractures.
Water prises those seams apart into steps and clean corners. And in forty years nobody has found a tool mark, a carving or a single artifact down there.

research.summary: In 1986 Kihachiro Aratake of the Yonaguni-Cho Tourism Association noticed stepped seabed formations while looking for hammerhead sharks about 26 m down below Arakawabana cliff at the southern tip of Yonaguni Island, roughly 100 km east of Taiwan. Masaaki Kimura of the University of the Ryukyus has argued the formations are man-made stepped monoliths - pyramid, castles, roads, monuments, stadium - revising his age estimate from 10,000 to 2,000-3,000 years; Wikipedia characterises these claims as pseudoarchaeological. The rock is Early Miocene Yaeyama Group sandstone and mudstone deposited about 20 million years ago. Robert Schoch, Wolf Wichmann and a 2019 study by Ogata and colleagues attribute the rectilinear, stepped appearance to weathering and erosion along parallel bedding planes and vertical joints. No artifacts have been reported; a 2024 Kyushu University team also reported no traces of human activity. Neither the Agency for Cultural Affairs nor Okinawa Prefecture recognises the site.

stories.description: A forty-ton boulder pulled from a Massachusetts river carries marks that have been read as Phoenician, Norse, Portuguese, Chinese and Indigenous. Every translation but one has collapsed, and the stone itself cannot be dated. #unsolvedmysteries #bizarrehistory #archaeology

factual_claims.text: At least five different origins have been proposed for Dighton Rock, a 40-ton sandstone boulder from the Taunton River in Berkley, Massachusetts.
Rev. John Danforth drew the petroglyphs in 1680, the drawing is held by the British Museum, and Cotton Mather described the rock in 1690.
Ezra Stiles proposed a Phoenician origin in 1783, Carl Christian Rafn a Norse origin in 1837, and Gavin Menzies a Chinese origin in 2002.
Edmund Delabarre of Brown University read the inscription as naming Miguel Corte-Real and the year 1511, and Douglas Hunter debunked that reading in 2017.

segments.narration: Five different civilisations have been credited with carving one boulder. Dighton Rock. Forty tons of sandstone, hauled out of a river in Massachusetts.
A minister sketched its marks in 1680, and that drawing sits in the British Museum. Cotton Mather wrote the rock up ten years later.
Then the readings began. Phoenician letters, said Ezra Stiles in 1783. Norsemen, said a Danish scholar in 1837. Chinese sailors, said an author in 2002.
A Brown University professor found a Portuguese name in the scratches: Miguel Corte-Real, 1511. A 2017 book pulled that apart line by line.
No translation has survived scrutiny. The marks look like the Indigenous petroglyphs found across New England, and the mineral crust grown into the carvings means nobody can date them.

research.summary: Dighton Rock is a roughly 40-ton sandstone boulder, about 5 ft high by 9.5 ft wide by 11 ft long, originally in the Taunton River at Berkley, Massachusetts. Rev. John Danforth drew its petroglyphs in 1680 (drawing in the British Museum) and Cotton Mather described it in 1690; Greenwood's 1730 account is called the first reliable description. Proposed origins include Native American (Danforth's own view), Phoenician (Ezra Stiles, 1783), Norse (Carl Christian Rafn, 1837, rejected by Kendrick and Feder), Portuguese/Miguel Corte-Real (Edmund Delabarre, from 1912, debunked by Douglas Hunter in 2017), and Chinese (Gavin Menzies, 2002). State officials removed the rock from the river in 1963 during coffer-dam construction and it now sits in a museum at Dighton Rock State Park; it was listed on the National Register in 1980. Wikipedia still describes the carvings as of uncertain origin, and surface weathering plus mineral crusts in the carved grooves prevent accurate dating - which is why the script presents the Indigenous reading as the surviving one rather than as settled.

factual_claims.text: Fly Geyser, on Fly Ranch in Washoe County, Nevada, was created accidentally and has been active since a 1964 well drilling.
A geothermal company drilled a well there in 1964, found the water not hot enough to use, reportedly capped it, and the seal failed.
The escaping water carries dissolved calcium carbonate and silica, which it deposits around the vent.
Those deposits built the geyser's cones and travertine pools, with the whole mound reported at roughly 25 to 30 feet.
The green and red colours come from thermophilic microbes, and the Burning Man Project bought the 3,800-acre Fly Ranch in June 2016 for $6.5 million.

segments.narration: Nevada drilled for power and accidentally built a geyser. Fly Ranch, in the desert west of the Black Rock. It has not stopped since 1964.
A geothermal company sank a well there, found the water too cool to be worth anything, and capped it off. The seal failed.
Hot water has been pushing out of it ever since, loaded with dissolved calcium carbonate and silica. And every litre leaves a little of that behind.
So it is still growing. Mineral cones, stepped pools, a mound now roughly thirty feet, built by a mistake nobody fixed.
The scarlet and green are heat-loving microbes living in the runoff. In 2016 Burning Man's nonprofit bought the entire ranch, geyser included, for six and a half million dollars.

research.summary: Fly Geyser sits on private land at Fly Ranch in Washoe County, Nevada, in the Hualapai Flat geothermal area west of the Black Rock Desert. A 1916 irrigation well hit near-boiling geothermal water and formed a calcium-carbonate cone about 10-12 ft tall. In 1964 a geothermal energy company drilled a second well nearby, found the water not hot enough for power, reportedly capped it, and the seal failed; the release reduced or dried the original geyser and dissolved calcium carbonate and silica began building the present cones and travertine pools. Sources are inconsistent on size (introduction: mound about 5 ft high by 12 ft wide; origin section: cones about 6 ft, whole mound 25-30 ft) so the script uses the 25-30 ft figure for the whole structure and avoids a jet-height claim. The green and red colours are attributed to thermophilic algae, bacteria and archaea. The nonprofit Burning Man Project bought the 3,800-acre ranch in June 2016 for $6.5 million; limited public access began in May 2018.

factual_claims.text: The eleven rock-hewn churches at Lalibela in Amhara, Ethiopia, were carved downward out of living rock rather than built up from blocks.
Workers cut trenches around the structures with hammers and chisels in scoriaceous basalt, carving top-down so the lowest part is cut last.
Four of the eleven are free-standing monoliths, tunnels link the church groups, and Biete Giorgis is cruciform in plan.
Tradition attributes the churches to King Gebre Meskel Lalibela, reigning about 1181 to 1221, and holds that the eleven took twenty-four years.

Archaeologist David Phillipson dates the oldest rock-hewn features at Lalibela to the 7th or 8th centuries, and scholars generally see four or five construction phases between the 7th and 13th centuries.

segments.narration: Eleven churches in Ethiopia were carved downward out of bedrock. Lalibela, up in the Amhara highlands. No blocks, no mortar, no scaffolding.
Crews cut trenches straight down into volcanic rock, then hollowed out the block they had left standing in the middle. Roof first. Floor last.
Four of them stand completely free of the mountain. Tunnels run between the groups. One, Bete Giyorgis, is a giant cross sunk into the ground.
Tradition gives all of it to one king, Gebre Meskel Lalibela, around 1200, and says the eleven took twenty-four years. The rock disagrees.
Archaeologist David Phillipson dated the earliest cuttings to the seventh or eighth century. Four or five building phases, five hundred years of work, and one king's name on the whole thing.

research.summary: Lalibela, in Amhara, Ethiopia, holds eleven medieval rock-hewn churches: four free-standing monoliths and seven still attached to the mountain, carved downward from living scoriaceous basalt with hammers and chisels, with trenches around them and tunnels linking two of the groups. Biete Giorgis is cruciform and free-standing. Tradition credits the Zagwe king Gebre Meskel Lalibela (reign c. 1181-1221) and holds the eleven took 24 years, with the town conceived as a second Jerusalem. Cambridge archaeologist David Phillipson argues the oldest rock-hewn features may date to the 7th or 8th centuries, about 500 years earlier than the traditional dating, with the last phase under the king whose name the town bears; the Metropolitan Museum states scholars generally agree on four or five phases between the 7th and 13th centuries. UNESCO inscribed the site in 1978. The local legend recorded by the sources checked involves Christ and Jerusalem, not angels, so no angel legend appears in the script.

factual_claims.text: A coelacanth, a fish thought extinct for about 66 million years, was caught off South Africa near the Chalumna River in December 1938 in the catch of the trawler Nerine.
Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, curator of the East London Museum, spotted the fish in the catch and sent drawings to Rhodes University.
Ichthyologist J. L. B. Smith replied by cable: 'Most important preserve skeleton and gills'.
Smith offered a reward of 100 pounds for a second coelacanth and one was found off the Comoros in December 1952.
Between 1938 and 1975, 84 coelacanth specimens were recorded, they live on deep reef and volcanic slopes, and two living species of Latimeria are known.

segments.narration: Fishermen landed a fish extinct for sixty-six million years. December 1938, off South Africa's coast. The trawler Nerine, hauling near the Chalumna River.

segments.narration: Museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer saw it in the catch. Blue, heavy, limbs where fins should be. She sketched it and cabled a university.
The reply: most important, preserve skeleton and gills. Ichthyologist J. L. B. Smith had seen this body plan only in Cretaceous rock. How was it swimming?
Smith printed leaflets across the region offering a hundred pounds for another. Fourteen years passed. Then, December 1952, one surfaced in the Comoros.
It was never extinct. Coelacanths live on steep volcanic slopes, too deep for old nets. Eighty-four turned up by 1975. Two species survive today.

research.summary: The coelacanth was known only from the fossil record and assumed to have died out at the end of the Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago, until 22 December 1938, when East London Museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer found one in the catch of the trawler Nerine near the Chalumna River in South Africa. J. L. B. Smith of Rhodes University named it Latimeria chalumnae and spent years circulating a 100-pound reward for a second specimen; it came from the Comoros in December 1952. The animal was never extinct, only living where the nets of the time did not reach: 84 specimens were recorded between 1938 and 1975, and a second living species was recognised in Indonesia in 1997.

stories.title: Kazakhstan Has A Forest That Stands Up Underwater
stories.description: Two thousand metres up in the Tian Shan, bleached spruce trunks rise straight out of a mountain lake with a whole drowned forest below them. Guidebooks credited a 1911 earthquake for a century, until the trees' own growth rings gave a different year. #lakekaindy #kazakhstan #bizarrehistory
stories.editorial_rationale: Tunnel of Eupalinos (hook 110.7%) scored by stating a plainly impossible physical scene in one flat sentence, so this hook states the standing underwater forest outright instead of teasing it as something strange in a lake.

factual_claims.text: Lake Kaindy in southern Kazakhstan sits about 2,000 m above sea level and holds a submerged forest of upright spruce trunks.
The drowned trees are Schrenk spruce, Picea schrenkiana, and their exposed upper trunks have lost bark and branches and turned white.
The lake formed when a limestone landslide dammed the gorge, cold water preserves the trunks, and the event was long attributed to the 1911 Kebin earthquake.
A tree-ring study compared the submerged trunks with living spruce on the surrounding slopes and dated the lake's formation to shortly after autumn 1888.
That study attributes the lake to the Chilik earthquake of 11 July 1889, magnitude 8.2, about 22 years earlier than the generally accepted date.

segments.narration: A spruce forest still stands upright underwater in Kazakhstan. Lake Kaindy, two thousand metres up in the Tian Shan, east of Almaty.
The trunks are Schrenk spruce. Branches and bark stripped away, bleached white, the tops breaking the surface like pale masts. Below, whole trees wait.
Cold mountain water keeps them from rotting. A limestone landslide dammed the gorge and drowned the valley. But when? Guidebooks all said 1911.
Then researchers compared rings from the dead trunks against living spruce on the slopes above. The dead trees stopped growing after autumn 1888.
That points to the Chilik earthquake of July 1889, magnitude 8.2, twenty-two years earlier than anyone thought. The trees dated their own drowning.

research.summary: Lake Kaindy, about 130 km east of Almaty in Kolsay Lakes National Park in the northern Tian Shan, is roughly 400 m long, up to 30 m deep and 2,000 m above sea level. It formed when a limestone landslide dammed a gorge and the valley filled, drowning a stand of Schrenk spruce whose trunks still stand upright; cold water has preserved them, while the parts above the surface lost bark and branches and bleached white. The formation was long credited to the 1911 Kebin earthquake. A tree-ring study by Miramont, Rizza and colleagues, published in Natural Hazards, cross-dated the submerged trunks against living spruce on the slopes and placed the drowning shortly after autumn 1888, pointing instead to the magnitude 8.2 Chilik earthquake of 11 July 1889, in whose epicentral zone the lake lies.

Fewer than sixty adults exist in the wild, every one of them genetically indistinguishable, and the exact location is still a secret. #wollemipine #australia #unsolvedmysteries

factual_claims.text: Genetic testing found all known wild Wollemi pines genetically indistinguishable from one another.
The Wollemi pine was found on about 10 September 1994 by David Noble with two companions exploring canyons in Wollemi National Park, about 150 km north-west of Sydney.

The tree's pollen matches fossil pollen named Dilwynites, recorded across the southern continents from roughly 90 million years ago, and fewer than 60 adult wild trees are known across four locations.
The genetic uniformity is consistent with a bottleneck 10,000 to 26,000 years ago that may have cut the population to one or two individuals.
The grove's exact location is undisclosed, and during the 2019-2020 bushfire season specialist crews installed irrigation and dropped retardant to save it.

segments.narration: September 1994. David Noble and two friends roped into an unexplored canyon and found trees with bubbly bark and ferny leaves. Nobody recognised them.
Botanists matched their pollen to fossil pollen from drill cores across the southern continents, stretching back ninety million years. So why only sixty trees?
Genetics answered it. A bottleneck within the last twenty-six thousand years cut them to perhaps one or two individuals. Every living tree descends from those.
The exact site stays secret. When the 2019 bushfires closed in, specialist crews flew in, laid irrigation lines and dropped retardant. The grove held.

research.summary: Wollemia nobilis was found on about 10 September 1994 by David Noble, Michael Casteleyn and Tony Zimmerman while exploring canyons in Wollemi National Park, about 150 km north-west of Sydney; the find was kept under official secrecy for months and the grove's location is still undisclosed. Fewer than 60 adult trees are known across four sites, and genetic testing found them indistinguishable, consistent with a bottleneck 10,000-26,000 years ago that may have reduced the population to one or two individuals. The tree's pollen matches the fossil pollen genus Dilwynites, recorded across Australia, New Zealand, Antarctica and South America from roughly 90 million years ago to about 2 million years ago. The species is listed Critically Endangered, and specialist National Parks crews with irrigation lines and retardant drops saved the grove in the 2019-2020 bushfires.

stories.description: New Zealand's Pink and White Terraces drew Victorian travellers from the other side of the world, until Mount Tarawera tore a seventeen-kilometre rift across the lake they sat on. A survey diary found in a Basel archive reopened the hunt for them 150 years later. #pinkandwhiteterraces #newzealand #unsolvedmysteries

factual_claims.text: Mount Tarawera erupted on 10 June 1886, opening a 17 km rift across the mountain and Lake Rotomahana and destroying the Pink and White Terraces.
The White Terraces covered about 8 hectares in roughly 50 layers descending about 25 m, and the terraces were New Zealand's most famous tourist attraction.
The eruption left a crater more than 100 m deep that filled with water, forming a lake 30 to 40 m higher than the old one.

Ferdinand von Hochstetter's 1859 survey is considered the most accurate record of the pre-eruption lake, and his field diary was found in the Hochstetter Collection Basel when Sascha Nolden took up its curation in 2010.

Bunn and Nolden's 2017 paper placed the terraces buried 10 to 15 m underground near the shoreline, while GNS Science, Bill Keir and a later NIWA reconstruction using the diary and lidar place the former sites beneath the modern lake.

segments.narration: Fifty stone terraces vanished in a single night. Lake Rotomahana, New Zealand, the tenth of June 1886. Mount Tarawera tore open a seventeen-kilometre rift.
Before that, the Pink and White Terraces were the country's great attraction. Silica staircases, dropping twenty-five metres over fifty basins of warm water.
Victorians sailed the world to bathe there. Then the crater filled and the lake rose thirty to forty metres. Where exactly had the terraces been?
In 2010 an archivist in Basel opened Ferdinand von Hochstetter's 1859 survey diary. His bearings were the last accurate fix on the lost shoreline.
Two teams read it differently: buried under the shore, or drowned by the new lake. The latest reconstruction, diary plus lidar, puts them underwater.

research.summary: The Pink and White Terraces were silica terraces on Lake Rotomahana in New Zealand's Bay of Plenty and the country's most famous tourist attraction, the White Terraces covering about 8 hectares in roughly 50 layers falling about 25 m. The Mount Tarawera eruption of 10 June 1886 opened a 17 km rift across the mountain and the lake, left a crater over 100 m deep and raised the refilled lake 30-40 m. Ferdinand von Hochstetter's 1859 survey remains the most accurate record of the old lake; his field diary surfaced in the Hochstetter Collection Basel when Sascha Nolden took up its curation in 2010 and was given to Rex Bunn in 2016. Bunn and Nolden's 2017 paper in the Journal of the Royal Society of New Zealand argued the terraces lie buried 10-15 m below the present shoreline and could be excavated; GNS Science, Bill Keir (2017) and de Ronde, Tontini and Keam (2018) disputed it, and NIWA's reconstruction using the same diary with lidar places the former sites beneath the modern lake.

factual_claims.text: The Thames Tunnel, begun in February 1825 between Rotherhithe and Wapping and about 400 metres long, flooded six times during construction before opening on 25 March 1843.
A flood on 12 January 1828 killed six men, and Isambard Kingdom Brunel survived it.
Marc Brunel patented the tunnelling shield in January 1818; it was divided into compartments with one worker per cell and the brickwork was placed behind it as it advanced.
The shield's design is widely credited to the shipworm Teredo navalis, which bores through ship timber behind a hard shell and lines its burrow as it goes.
The tunnel drew about two million pedestrians a year paying a penny, was converted to a railway in 1869, and has carried London Overground trains since 2010.

segments.narration: The Thames flooded this tunnel six times before it opened. Rotherhithe to Wapping, started 1825, four hundred metres of brick under a tidal river.
Nobody had tunnelled under a navigable river before. The bed was soft silt, dig in and the river poured through. Six men died in 1828.
Marc Brunel's answer was patented in 1818: an iron shield, divided into cells, one miner per cell, brickwork laid right behind as it crept forward.
Engineers long credited the idea to a dockyard pest: the shipworm, which bores through ship timber behind a hard shell, lining the hole as it goes.
It worked. Two million people a year paid a penny to walk under the Thames. Overground trains still run through Brunel's brick tube.

research.summary: Marc Brunel and his son Isambard built the Thames Tunnel between Rotherhithe and Wapping from February 1825, 400 m long and about 23 m below the river at high tide, at a cost of roughly 454,000 pounds to dig and 180,000 to fit out. The river broke in six times during construction, on 18 May 1827, 12 January 1828 (killing six men, with Isambard surviving), 23 August and 3 November 1837, 20 March 1838 and 3 April 1840. The work was only possible because of the tunnelling shield Marc Brunel patented with Lord Cochrane in January 1818: an iron frame divided into compartments, one worker per cell advancing independently with brickwork laid behind. The shield's inspiration is widely credited to the shipworm Teredo navalis, which Brunel encountered at Chatham Dockyard; the attribution is traditional rather than documented by Brunel himself. The tunnel opened on 25 March 1843, drew about two million penny-paying pedestrians a year, became a railway tunnel in 1869 and has carried London Overground trains since 27 April 2010.
